a) Overview of grid-like sampling strategy for tumour AT15. b) Distributions of common RNA QC metrics (number of genes by counts, total counts, mitochondrial read fraction, and doublet scores) post-filtering across major coarse-grained cell states. Boxplots display median, IQR, and 1.5x IQR whiskers for n = 1,025,329 nuclei summarised across n = 155 10X reactions. c) Summary of ATAC QC metrics and applied QC filters. From left to right: nuclei passing generic ArchR filters, nuclei passing both generic ArchR filters and RNA filters, and promoter ratio compared against minimum fragments.Generic ArchR filters indicated by solid lines (minimum unique fragments ≥ 1000 and TSS enrichments ≥ 4). Dashed lines represent target minimum values for the respective metrics.

a) Visium ST sections from each sampling site of tumour AT10 coloured according to GB cell state abundances derived from cell2location mapping. The top seven most frequently observed states at the tumour-level were visualised, with colour intensity proportional to inferred cell state abundance. Broader trends, particularly areas of cell state co-localisation are highlighted in bold text. b) Images depict overlayed cell2location-derived cell state abundances (colour intensity) for the highest-abundance cell states (colour) across each tumour. The top 7 cell states were selected on the basis of ranked maximum abundance. One section from a single site was included (top left).

a) Tissue microenvironment summaries. Left: Most frequently observed cell state (column) found within each microenvironment (row). Dotplot shows the proportion of the top cell state per spatial microenvironment averaged across tumours (size) and the average Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) across tumours. Centre: Relative frequency of each microenvironment across tumours (size and colour). Right: Correlation of spatial microenvironments with histopathological features annotated on Visium H&E images based on IvyGAP annotations (columns). Dotplot shows the proportion of spots associated with a spatial microenvironment which overlap with a given histological feature (size) and the point biserial correlation coefficient (r) between feature annotations and spatial microenvironment abundance. b) Tissue microenvironment (colour) abundance (colour intensity) overlaid on Visium H&Es for a subset of patients, demonstrating microenvironment regionalisation. Microenvironments with the highest max abundance were visualised.

a) Dotplot depicting common EMT markers compared to markers associated with astrogliosis. Colour intensity is the mean expression across a cell state with min-max normalisation applied across each gene. Dot size corresponds to the proportion of cells in a group expressing a given gene (expression greater than 0). Colours correspond to groups of EMT-associated genes and genes associated with both EMT and astrogliosis (including “Astrogliosis pathways”). b) Immunofluorescent staining of GB tissue section revealing distinct patterns of AKAP12 (AC-gliosis) and HILPDA (hypoxic) protein expression. Panels show single channels of a region of interest (scale bar: 100 µm). Imaging performed for n = 3 tumours, independently. c) Xenium section demonstrating zonation of AC-gliosis-hypoxia cell states ranging from infiltrated grey matter to the necrotic tumour core.

a) LCM-informed CNA calling workflow to predict snRNA-seq CN events via alleleIntegrator. The scatterplot (top right) represents the B-allele frequency (BAF) for sample PD60966a_lo0005. Colours correspond to SNP allele frequency of the major (red) and minor (blue) alleles. The UMAP (bottom right) shows alleleIntegrator clone calls superimposed on the visualisation such that cells with chr17 CNs (light blue) can be distinguished from cells without chr17 CNs (orange). b) Barplots depicting cell state distributions across clones (right) and clone distribution across tumour sampling sites (left) in LCM-WGS informed clones. c) Sankey plot depicting concordant clone assignment across multiome and LCM-informed CNA calling methods per cell. d) Phylogeny of SNV clusters across AT3 LCM-WGS samples. Branch length corresponds to mutation counts on a natural logarithmic scale. Clusters are coloured according to their cluster IDs in Fig. 4e. Mutation counts associated with each SNV cluster are indicated in square brackets. e) Analysis of clonal intermixture using Rao’s quadratic entropy (Rao’s Q). Rao’s Q is displayed for each LCM ROI (columns). Tree-bound SNV cluster frequencies (right) are also depicted, showing the relative distribution of SNV clusters nested in a phylogenetic context. f) LCM-WGS- and SpaceTree-based spatial clone mapping workflows. g) Spatial clonal domains compared across LCM-WGS pyclone deconvolution and Visium ST SpaceTree mapping across matching tissue locations. Domains were defined by Bray-Curtis clustering of clone distributions within each ROI across each modality. H&E images depict tissue locations used for LCM colored by SpaceTree clone clusters (left) and pyclone-VI clone clusters (right). The sankey plot demonstrates ROI cluster assignment between modalities. h) SpaceTree distinguishes tumour versus normal regions and resolves spatial clonal domains in tumours. Top: Visium section from tumour AT15 showing SpaceTree mapping of diploid versus malignant subclones to infiltrated and bulk tumour regions, respectively. Bottom: Spatial clonal domains identified by clustering SpaceTree-derived clonal composition of Visium spots. i) SpaceTree cell state (left) and clonal (centre and right) maps of tumour AT10 resolves distinct regional distributions of the chr17-CNA subclone. j) Tumour purity of infiltrated versus tumour tissue microenvironments estimated by SpaceTree, summarised at the Visium spot level (n = 97 Visium sections). Boxplots display median, IQR, and 1.5x IQR whiskers.

a) Cellular trajectory analysis workflow. b) Scatterplot depicting major QC metrics for cell2fate trajectory results. Patches correspond to QC thresholds: maximum latent time > 25 (red), and average transition score > 0.2 (yellow). Trajectories below the maximum latent time threshold (grey) were omitted from analysis, and those passing were used (blue) but flagged if they fell beneath the transition score threshold. c) Clones which passed trajectory QC thresholds (blue) compared to those which were omitted (grey) for each tumour. d) Boxplot summarising min-max normalised latent time for each cell state across all clones passing QC thresholds (A). Box colour corresponds to cell class. Boxplots display median, IQR, and 1.5x IQR whiskers (n = 88,495 cells across n = 11 high-diversity clones). e) Boxplot summarising transition scores between granular cell states in among clones passing cell2fate QC threshold (Extended Data Fig. 6b). Transitions (x-axis) are denoted by “>” and are ordered such that the first cell state transitions into the second. Colours (shared with Extended Data Fig. 6d) correspond to the cell classes involved in the transition. Boxplots colours are split by source (left) and target (right) cell classes. The red dashed line represents the threshold for transition scores used during QC. Boxplots show median, IQR, and 1.5x IQR whiskers (n = 559 total observed cell state transitions across a total of 23 clones).

a) Histograms showing cell class distribution across latent time for each clone passing QC thresholds. Colours correspond to cell class. The x-axis represents min-max normalised latent time.

a) Recurrent temporal gene expression modules are conserved across the trajectories of 23 tumour subclones. Heatmap (left) displays top marker gene overlap (n = 200) across factors associated with each meta-module. Colour bars correspond to marker overlap proportion and average latent time across each recurrent module. Additional heatmap (right) depicts the cell2fate meta-module enrichment among coarse-grained states. Colour corresponds to z-score normalised mean relative expression scores for each cell state. Rows are shared between heatmaps and ordered by average min-max normalised latent time observed across each meta-module. b) Spatial mapping of key temporal modules (colours) from subclone AT15_4 onto its matching Visium section (right). Network diagram (bottom) shows the mean pairwise euclidean distance between temporal modules for the associated Visium section. c) Activation patterns of genes (top) and meta-modules (bottom) for clone AT15_3 summarising the inferred cellular trajectory. Cell2fate derived activation plots of temporal gene expression modules (top) and top marker genes of each module (bottom) with matched colours. d) Example of TF expression rate over time for TFs implicated in three different stages of inferred latent time across three clones (AT9_2, AT15_3, and AT4_1): early time (top), mid-range time (middle), and late time (bottom) TFs. Line plots are summarising TF rate across all stated clones. Colours correspond to TF identity.

a) GFP epifluorescence images of D7 GBOs infiltrated by E25 and E30 GB cell lines (left) and close up images of infiltrating single cells (right). Right, top panel: Epifluorescence image showing GBO infiltration at D7. Right, bottom panel: GFP transcripts (green spots) marking engrafted cells overlaid on Xenium images showing DAPI (blue) and cell segmentation panel (pink-yellow-green). Scale bars: 500 µm (top), 20 µm (bottom). Imaging performed for n = 3 independent GBOs. b) UMAPs summarising scVI integration of our cell atlas with GBO data (left) and scANVI label transfer results using our coarse-grained cell state annotation (right). c) Dotplots showing expression of GB cell state marker genes in our Xenium data for cell state identifies transferred using scANVI. Dot size corresponds to the proportion of cells expressing a gene within a given group, dot colour corresponds to normalised expression within a given group (see legend at bottom of panel). Plots show GBO and engrafted cells pooled across all timepoints. d) Spatial plots showing zonated cell state organisation of GBOs using label-transferred cell state identities (top) and marker gene expression (bottom). Marker gene expression colour intensity maps to log1p normalised gene expression as indicated by colourbars. e) Line plot summarising cell state proportions of GFP+ engrafted cells across E25 (top) and E30 (bottom) organoids for each time point. Points correspond to proportions from individual organoids. Colour corresponds to the data modalities, where pre-engrafted scRNA-seq are indicated in orange, and GFP+ cells mapped via Xenium are indicated in blue.

a) Myeloid heterogeneity in our multimodal atlas. Dendrogram depicts transcriptomic clustering of myeloid subcluster snRNA-seq profiles annotated to three major phenotypic classes (background colors). Stacked bar plots depict the relative distribution of myeloid states across tumours and the proportion of top myeloid activity signatures from Miller at al. per state. Dotplots show key marker gene expression and selected term enrichment across states. The spatial correlation dotplot depicts the enrichment of myeloid cell states in cell2location TMs (prop) and the Pearson correlation coefficient between cell state abundances and TM niche abundance (r). b) Spatial co-localisation of distinct malignant and myeloid states. Visium sections (left) show cell2location abundances of top cell states in tumour AT15 with colours mapping to corresponding labels highlighted in the boxes to the right. Malignant cell states are grouped according to their trajectory and myeloid cell states are grouped according to their phenotypic classes and their spatial organisation. c) Schematic detailing the spatially resolved cell-cell communication analysis strategy to detect signalling from distinct myeloid subtypes to their spatially co-localised malignant states that recur across multiple tumours. d) Myeloid ligands predicted to signal to distinct malignant cell states by spatially-resolved cell-cell communication analysis. Genes correspond to top ligands identified in myeloid signalling factors identified by tensor decomposition analysis. Dotplot represents the proportion of myeloid cells expressing the ligand (size) and relative expression across cell states (colour). e) Overview of major cell-cell interactions identified between regional myeloid (sender) and distinct malignant (receiver) cell states.

#1384. Man United 3-2 Roma PLAYER RATINGS: Which star delivered their best performance in a red shirt? Whose physicality is something to marvel at? And who deserves 3/10 for their abysmal defending?

Published: 17:21 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 11:18 EDT, 4 November 2026

Manchester United pulled out an enormous win for Michael Carrick as they fought back from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League.

Winless in nine games heading into this European night under the lights and United were staring at 10 without a win, a record that was last struck in 1978, when they were two down at half-time after a dreadful start.

But United conjured up spirit that has been barely visible so far this season as a brace from Matheus Cunha - who finished the night getting sent off - followed a penalty from Bruno Fernandes to seal the most crucial of wins.

What it means for Carrick's future in the medium to longer term remains to be seen.

Those upstairs at United have privately taken a lot of the blame and want to end the churn of managers carrying the can for poor player performances. Only time will tell how big a turning point this night can be.

Daily Mail Sport's NATHAN SALT was at Old Trafford on a frantic night to run the rule over the players...

Matheus Cunha rescued victory from the jaws of defeat for Manchester United against Roma

Made a big save low to his right on the stroke of half-time to prevent further embarrassment for United and, as it turned out, give them a fighting chance of getting the result they pulled out of the hat. His distribution seems to have really regressed this season with far too many aimless balls, though.

Made a huge recovery tackle to deny Rodrigo Mora a third and in a feckless first half it was he who bust a gut where others didn't. Yes, it's a low bar but Yoro has actually been one of, if not, the best United performers during this never-ending malaise.

A performance littered with mistakes that, in truth, looked to have been scrubbed from his game coming into this campaign. He's the leader of the back-line and he did everything but lead in a first half that saw positioning and decision-making leave a lot to be desired. His clearance that resulted in Roma's second goal was diabolical. Booked and was fortunate not to have been sent off.

Harry Maguire left a lot to be desired in a defensive performance littered with basic errors

Thrust into the side in place of Lisandro Martinez and his head will have been spinning when he gave away a penalty for a handball, which Donyell Malen converted. Booked for a lunging challenge that is becoming a worrying trend of tackling with studs up. May sound daft but he needs coaching by Jonny Evans or Jonathan Woodgate on a better way to slide tackle. Booked.

Abysmal defending for Roma's first goal as he committed to the attack like a winger and left Matias Soule the freedom of Manchester to score. Kept pushing forward – you have to assume by instruction – and kept being found wanting. Options are slim but he's not making any positive contribution to the team from left back. Needs a stop putting to it.

Got told to 'f**k off' by Bruno Fernandes in a fraught first half for a bobbly pass to tee him up on the edge of the box. Made a couple of smart bursts through lines but he's in the side to protect the defence and he didn't do it. Night cut short when he pulled his hamstring 60 seconds into the second half.

Will be disappointed with himself at how sloppily he gave away the ball in a turnover which exposed his defenders for the first goal. That error aside, he settled in and improved as it wore on. His ability to actually beat a man is in short supply in this United side and his physicality was something to marvel at at times.

Kobbie Mainoo actually looks to drive past players, a skill in short supply at United

Always has a buzz about him when he gets the ball and he was the only one to come back from Como with any crumb of credit. Here it was a more sobering affair where his influence was heavily restricted and it means his wait for a United goal goes on. Not managed one since December 2025.

A night of frustration for large spells but one that did eventually serve up a goal and assist for the United captain. He was unfairly booked when Soule got into a pushing match that was very one sided down in the corner. Missed a second-half penalty (which was re-taken due to encroachment) and made no mistake second time around. All that aside, it was a poor look when he's berating team-mates when his own performance level is way below what he's capable of, mind you.

Comfortably the best player in a United shirt on the night - even with the red card. For one, he gets stuck in. For two, it was Cunha who won the penalty – however fortunate a decision that was – that Fernandes eventually converted to make it 2-1. He deserved an assist when he set Mbeumo free for a run on goal moments later. Scored two crucial late goals that will airbrush just how bad a tackle he made to see red. Could make a case for his best performance in a United shirt. It's up there.

Had his head in his hands, much like a lot of the supporters, when he struck both posts after being played through one v one by Cunha. Had a couple of opportunities to scamper through on goal but just didn't have the pace.

Bryan Mbeumo will want his second half breakaway chance back after striking both posts

Muted in celebration at the end and given everything he's had to navigate this season that's perhaps understandable. But this was a shot in the arm, how big we need to wait and see. People have labelled him a dead man walking but he's not giving up yet.

Youri Tielemans (for Carlos Baleba, 51) - 5

Did OK, but didn't do a great deal to drive the play forward. Not exactly the perfect foil to Mainoo, who is stylistically similar.

Lifted the crowd and helped change the game. Should have won a penalty when he was hacked down and it was his assist to Cunha that sealed victory. Coudln't have made a stronger case to start on Sunday.

Lisandro Martinez (for Ayden Heaven, 75) - 6

The fact he was far away from the eventual headlines was probably a good thing for all concerned after what transpired at Stamford Bridge.

Vasquez 6; Mancini 6 (Ghilardi 76, 5), Balerdi 4, Hermoso 5 (N'Dicka 76, 5); Rensch 5 (Lulli 21, 6), Cristante 6, De Roon 7, Franca 6; Mora 8, Malen 7 (Castro 78), Soule 7

#1383. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

Désiré Doué with a brilliant finish from range to give PSG an early lead in Manchester 😮‍💨 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/Uwilx7I37H

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City’s run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned, but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching financial fair play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

So we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Not that he savoured much of what he saw as PSG dominated City to such an extent that their fans adopted the “Poznan” celebration and the home supporters were silenced.

City could have gone in front before they conceded with the erratic Safonov – who was Gianluigi Donnarumma’s understudy and has become his unlikely replacement – punching a corner against his own crossbar before Antoine Semenyo shot the rebound over.

Then PSG ran all over City. They broke far too easily and scored far too easily. Not once, but twice, to go 2-0 up.

For the first, PSG countered, with City struggling to cover, and Doué caught out Donnarumma with a low shot inside his right-hand post from 22 yards.

Then PSG sliced through City’s defence with Ousmane Dembélé scooping the ball across the area to Doué who returned it back. Dembélé stooped to head home.

Ousmane Dembélé doubles PSG's lead just 2 minutes after they scored the first 🤯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/MxhJ3oCWpC

After Achraf Hakimi headed against the inside of a post and City could not clear, the ball came back with Warren Zaïre-Emery flicking on Maghnes Akliouche’s cut-back. It ran to Vitinha who slammed in a first-time shot. It was the first time City had ever conceded three goals at home in the first half of this competition.

Vitinha with a BEAUTY to put PSG three up after just 30 minutes 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/vgqkI6kI3h

Maybe it was too easy. Maybe City could not continue to be so dominated but it was as if a switch was flicked when the teams returned. The chances came for City. Enzo Fernández should have scored from a close-range header and Haaland did, glancing in an inswinging Ndiaye cross.

Finally the City fans found their voices but then they were silenced. What a calamity for Donnarumma as he got a hand to Akliouche’s shot on the turn, but only palmed the ball up in the air before it bounced into the net.

But City did not stop. Nuno Mendes headed Josko Gvardiol’s flick off the line, Fernández hit a post before Bouaddi set up Haaland and he swept the ball past Safonov.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

There was time for PSG to miss a penalty, with Donnarumma comfortably saving Ferran Torres’s weak effort as City bravely continued to push. They lost, but it did not quite feel like that.

Former manager joins chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano in the directors’ box.

Pep Guardiola, wearing a flat cap, has taken his seat in the Manchester City directors’ box, directly behind chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana. It is of course his first game back at the club after quitting as manager in the summer. It is also a declared show of solidarity after the guilty verdict.

It’s a special night against the best team in Europe, I hope it’s a special game. Pep is here but was not at the training ground. I have not spoken with him.

It’s a special moment for him also, he is back in his home and the fans will be happy that he is here tonight.

Quite easy decision to bring Jérémy in. The most important think for him is to stay fit that’s why he are having to manage his minutes.

I said yesterday you need a complete performance, top on and off the ball to beat them. We will create some chances and concede some chances but you have to find the complete balance.

Under normal circumstances there would be a high level of anticipation around this game, even though it is the eighth time in 11 seasons that City and PSG have faced each other in the Champions League. But given the backdrop of City guilty verdict and it being the first home fixture since that announcement it is even more fascinating. There will also be, of course, Pep Guardiola back “in his house”, as his successor, Enzo Maresca. put it. The atmosphere will be interesting.

If the verdicts are upheld, of course, it wasn’t their penthouse and it wasn’t their caviar.

We got to live in a penthouse and eat caviar for 15 years and if we have to go back to a semi in the suburbs, well, fine.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

And it didn’t go very well. Joe Cole was remarkably incoherent even for a football pundit talking about more important issues. And words you never thought you would type: Martin Keown the voice of sense:

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

PSG have made a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign, their worst since Luis Enrique’s first season in charge. Starting with two draws and a defeat, they have rallied with three successive victories to climb up to sixth as the head coach, as he tends to do in the league, rotates his midfielders and forwards like crazy, to whose ranks he has added the World Cup-winner Ferran Torres. The summer signing scored a hat-trick in his Champions League debut for the club, a 6-1 mauling of Slovan Bratislava.

City, too, started their European campaign with a win, Erling Haaland scoring both goals in the 2-0 victory over Porto at the Dragao and you won’t need me to remind you that they have won all six of their Premier League games to lead Arsenal by three points at the top of the table.

#1381. Michael Carrick might STILL be one game from the sack. A one-night stand of epic proportions was up there with Man United's best but produced more questions than answers, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 02:31 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 11:18 EDT, 4 November 2026

What a crazy, chaotic and, frankly, confusing night this was at Old Trafford. The grand old place has seen a few of them down the years, and Manchester United's incredible comeback win over Roma was right up there with the best.

By the end of it, the fans were loving United and hating the Glazers in keeping with their doctrine. Michael Carrick was savouring arguably his greatest moment as head coach, and yet might still be one game from the sack. Two-goal hero Matheus Cunha was being manhandled off the pitch and towards the tunnel, furious at not being able to celebrate with his teammates.

For Carrick, this felt like the equivalent of Erik ten Hag's win over Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final and Ruben Amorim's incredible 4-3 victory over Lyon in the Europa League quarter-final last year. The feelgood factor and sense of elation around Old Trafford was palpable.

Neither of those wins were enough to keep Ten Hag and Amorim in a job for much longer, and that is the conundrum for United bosses this morning.

If the feeling in the boardroom – and it remains an if – is to relieve Carrick of his duties, can they be swayed by a one-night stand, albeit one of epic proportions.

If United can follow this up with victory on Sunday over Aston Villa and Unai Emery – one of the candidates being touted as Carrick's replacement – can they really sack their head coach at the start of the international break?

Michael Carrick gave his players the half-time fire power needed to pull off a famous fightback

More than just pulling off the much-needed win against Roma, it felt as if his stars were playing for their manager

On another night when United fans turned on the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, director of football Jason Wilcox and even the players as boos greeted the half-time whistle and the 'play like you mean it' banner made a re-appearance for the first time in three years, it was a reminder that the most popular person at the club might be the man who is about to get the bullet.

The players certainly looked as though they are playing for Carrick, and afterwards Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans both gave him their backing.

Looking ahead to this game, Carrick had said: 'Whatever happens is going to happen after that in whatever direction it goes in, but we want to make it a big night tomorrow night first.'

Those words came true in spectacular fashion. For a while, it felt as though he wouldn't even survive until the Villa game as United's defence fell apart and Roma set a new record for a European opponent taking a two-goal lead at Old Trafford. It could have been worse.

Carrick got his players together at half-time and reminded them that it only takes one moment to light the touchpaper here. 'I don't like talking to the lads too much about the history of this place, but it's magical,' he said. 'There's something when we have these nights and we do it the hard way, and one moment can flip the whole feeling.'

Kobbie Mainoo put it more bluntly. 'We needed a bit of a kick,' said the United midfielder.

It worked. United roared back at Roma, showing a resolve and strength of character that has been missing for much of this season. Fernandes converted a retaken penalty, Cunha levelled and then smashed home the winner late on to give United their first victory in 10 games.

The Brazilian's sending-off for removing his shirt after scoring the third and then committing a silly foul on Leonardo Balerdi meant he wasn't allowed to go on the pitch at the end, much to his indignation. Carrick and his staff were there to reinforce the point.

Results clearly haven't been good enough this season, but one of the criticisms levelled at Carrick is that performances have been even worse. The combination of those two factors have left him fighting to save his job.

On the flip side, it felt like this win and the nature of it counted double. One that raised the roof at Old Trafford and lifted the soul.

Yet for so long on Tuesday night, the mood among the United faithful was one of mutiny. They revived the anti-Glazer campaign by bringing green and gold balloons into the Stretford End, and let them loose as the two teams walked out.

Rather like the protests against the absent owners who keep a safe distance thousands of miles away in America, they were never going to hit their target by reaching the pitch and floated harmlessly into the night air. A barrage of tennis balls had greater impact, but they too were soon cleared out of sight.

Chants against the Glazers, Ratcliffe and Wilcox rang out long before kick-off. 'You can stick your new stadium up your a***' chanted the fans. The game was seconds old when we heard the first rendition of 'sell United and f*** off home' followed by the tribute song to Carrick.

Even at a critical point in the game when VAR was studying Gianluca Mancini's challenge on Cunha to see if it warranted a penalty, the United fans broke into a chorus of 'we want Glazers out'. It was the same after Cunha fired the decisive goal as supporters turned on the Americans and voiced their support for Carrick once more. They were caught between wanting to vent their anger at the owners and back Carrick and the team.

Fervent and continuing protests against the ownership underscored Carrick's own popularity, despite being potentially days from getting the sack

Matheus Cunha might have been the late hero but he was unable to celebrate with his team-mates and manager after taking off his shirt

'The players one hundred per cent feed off the crowd, absolutely no doubt whatsoever,' said Carrick. 'I understand there's frustration and disappointment, I totally get that.

'Probably the time when it was easy for them not to be there, they were there. I felt that there was frustration, of course there was. I get it. But I know what they're like and we've got to give them something to go on.'

United managed to do that in the end, but it was a funny sort of night. One that produced more questions than answers. The biggest of them concerns Carrick. Is he doing enough to convince his employers that United can turn a corner? Victory in Europe doesn't alter the fact they are one place above the Premier League relegation zone.

There is one more game against Villa and then the choice is very simple: stick or twist?

#1380. Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3,4,5,6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

The gut microbiome exhibits large variations in its composition and genetic landscape. Within-species genetic variation underlies strain differences in fitness, metabolic capacities, pathogenicity and other biological properties. Thus, the field of microbiome research is moving towards strain-level or genetic-level dissection of the microbial contributions to human health (Supplementary Information). Structural variations in the gut microbiome have been linked to human body mass index (BMI), bile acid concentrations, the human plasma metabolome and host genetics, thereby identifying bacterial genes involved in glucose metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and biotransformation, and N-acetylgalactosamine utilization3,4,5,6.

However, gut microbial genomes also contain abundant SNVs that can modulate microbial function and host interactions. For example, a SNV in the blc gene of Escherichia coli disrupts the intestinal barrier by decreasing the amount of lysophosphatidylethanolamine, a metabolite that aids remission of inflammatory bowel disease7. In the stomach, a SNV in Helicobacter pylori increases gastric cancer risk by enhancing the proteolytic activity of the serine protease HtrA (ref. 8). In Bacteroides coprocola, SNVs in glycosyl hydrolase genes have been associated with type 2 diabetes9. A SNV-based metagenome-wide association study (SNV-MWAS) in an Israeli population identified BMI-associated SNVs that were replicated in a geographically independent Dutch cohort10. Despite these examples, systematic explorations of the relationships between gut microbial SNVs and host phenotypes have not, to our knowledge, been carried out at phenome-wide scale. Such analyses require large-scale human cohort data with both metagenomic and deep phenotypic data, and they need to overcome a number of technical challenges. For example, microbial species exhibit complex population genetic structures, and these strong lineage effects may lead to false discoveries in association studies if population structure is not properly controlled.

In this study, we compiled shotgun metagenomic sequencing data of 11,831 faecal samples from 5 independent cohorts from the Netherlands and a cohort from Tanzania. Gut microbial genotypes were characterized using GT-Pro11, yielding 12.8 million SNVs in core genomic regions. We further developed a linear mixed-model (LMM)-based analysis workflow that controls for within-species population genetic structure to ensure that SNV–phenome associations detected are independent from the cumulative effect of strain lineage. We then conducted a PheWAS to identify associations between common metagenomic SNVs and 244 host phenotypic and exposure factors, using LMM in each cohort, followed by meta-analysis. In total, we detected 940 independent association signals supported by multiple cohorts that link 39,663 SNVs across 101 species to 69 host phenotypes or exposures, and the full set of results are available in an online catalogue. We also performed protein structural analyses to interpret the biological relevance of these associations.

We compiled faecal metagenomic sequencing data for 11,831 samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 cohorts (Fig. 1). Five cohorts are from the Netherlands—the Dutch Microbiome Project (DMP; n = 7,955)12, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD; n = 1,135, plus 340 followed up after an average of 4 years (designated LLD1 for baseline samples and LLD2 for follow-up samples))3,13, the 500-Functional Genomics Project (500FG; n = 529)14,15, the 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Project (IBD; n = 544)16 and 300-Obesity (300OB; n = 298)15,17—and one is from Tanzania (300-Tanzania Functional Genomics Project (300TZFG), n = 320)18 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). For LLD2 and 500FG, we have additional datasets from some of the same individuals (nLLD2 = 251, nFG500 = 459) with samples processed using both DNA extraction methods19 that allowed us to assess the effect of extraction protocol on SNV profiling and the robustness of microbial genotyping (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1). The extensive phenotypic information for the corresponding samples was also curated and harmonized. We integrated 244 phenotypic and exposure factors (92 binary and 152 continuous or ordinal traits) available in the DMP or in at least 2 other cohorts for analysis (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 2). Among these, 131 phenotypes were available for at least 2 cohorts, whereas 113 were only available for the DMP. Across the whole dataset, the sample size per phenotype ranged from 593 to 11,706 (Supplementary Table 2).

In this study, we integrated whole-genome shotgun sequencing (WGS) data of 11,831 faecal samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts and harmonized 244 phenotype and exposure factors across these cohorts. Two of the six cohorts, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD) and 500-Functional Genomics (500FG), are represented by multiple datasets. n represents the number of faecal samples. LLD contains 1,135 samples collected at the study baseline time point (LLD1) and 340 samples collected for a subset of individuals at a follow-up time point after 4 years that were processed using two DNA isolation kits: 253 by QIAGEN QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (FSK; represented by circled F) (LLD2-FSK) and 338 using QIAGEN AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (APK; represented by circled A) (LLD2-APK). 500FG contains 529 samples that were also processed using the two DNA isolation kits: 517 processed using FSK (500FG-FSK) and 471 processed using APK (500FG-APK). To ensure sample independence in our downstream analysis, we used only LLD1 and 500FG-FSK in this analysis, and the additional datasets (LLD2-FSK, LLD2-APK and 500FG-APK) were used only to carry out technical assessments. We then conducted meta-genotyping for the WGS data from stool samples and generated the gut microbial genotype profile, keeping 12.8 million common biallelic microbial SNVs for the LMM-based SNV-MWAS. SNV-MWAS analyses were conducted separately for the six independent datasets from the six cohorts and then integrated through meta-analysis. Linkage disequilibrium-based grouping was conducted to extract independent signals, and an LMM-based permutation test was used to screen for robust association signals. To provide functional interpretation of SNV associations, we then carried out protein structural analysis. Created in BioRender; Fu, J. https://biorender.com/c1z5z7y (2026).

a, Overview of the 244 phenotype and exposure factors in this study. The proportions of samples with a non-missing value for the corresponding factor in each cohort are shown in the heat map. Each row represents a factor. Each column represents a cohort. b, Distributions of common SNV numbers of each species in each cohort. The numbers of species included were: DMP, n = 247; LLD1, n = 207; 500FG, n = 256; 300OB, n = 243; IBD, n = 154; and 300TZFG, n = 327. Inner box plots show summary statistics: the centre line represents the median, the box hinges represent the lower and upper quartiles of the distribution and whiskers extend no further than 1.5× interquartile range from the hinges, and data beyond the end of the whiskers are outliers plotted as individual points. c, Overall proportion of gut microbial SNV effect types.

We genotyped 50,945,657 biallelic SNVs in the core genome of 881 species using GT-Pro11, which conducts reference-panel-based SNV detection using k-mer searching and exact matching. The number of SNVs detected in the DMP was higher than in other cohorts, probably owing to its larger sample size (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). The total number of SNVs detected in at least 1 sample for each species ranged from 1 to 342,230 (mean = 58,131) (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The average density of SNVs in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 32 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1d), which is close to previous reports20. To keep only informative species for downstream analysis, we selected ‘common’ SNVs that were present in more than 10% of samples and had a minor allele frequency (MAF) of more than 5% in at least one cohort. Among the 50.95 million SNVs that were detected, 12,761,497 SNVs were common (Supplementary Table 3). As the distribution of common SNV counts per species was bimodal, with two peaks separated by approximately 1,000 SNVs (Extended Data Fig. 1e), we selected species with at least 1,000 common SNVs, resulting in 433 species with 12,706,564 common SNVs (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Table 4). These 433 species collectively accounted for, on average, 84.3% (s.d. = 9.4%) of the total abundance of the gut microbial community. After filtering, 300TZFG had the highest number of species for analysis (327) and the most common SNVs (7,369,266) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1f–h). The average density of common SNV sites in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 16 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1i). The within-species population structure of the 433 species and the effect of technical factors are described extensively in Supplementary Notes 2 and 3 (Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and Supplementary Tables 5–8). We also pre-calculated the Bonferroni-controlled threshold for study-wide significance by dividing 0.05 by the total number of phenotype–SNV pairs tested (922,497,753), yielding a threshold of 5.42 × 10−11 (Methods).

To understand the functional consequences of SNVs, we annotated genes from reference genomes and predicted the potential functional effect of SNVs on bacterial gene products (synonymous, missense, start or stop codon, and non-protein-coding)21 (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 9). Most SNVs (11,819,660, 93.02%) were located in protein-coding regions, including 9,579,907 (75.39%) synonymous, 2,216,969 (17.45%) missense and 22,784 (0.18%) start or stop codon variants (Fig. 2c). The distribution of the proportion of codon-altering SNVs (missense or start or stop codon SNVs) varied across different bacterial species (Extended Data Fig. 2), reflecting the genetic diversity and evolutionary pressures experienced by these species.

We next performed an SNV-MWAS of 244 factors by linking them to 12 million common SNVs using LMMs fitted separately for each species, phenotype and cohort. These LMMs controlled for population structure by including the species-level between-sample genetic linkage matrix as a random effect. Age, sex, species abundance and clean read count were included as fixed-effect covariates, except in the analyses for age and sex themselves. Given that reference and alternative alleles may coexist within a sample with differing abundances, we encoded gut microbial genotypes as a dosage value ranging from 0 to 1 to represent the frequency of the alternative allele.

Following the per-cohort SNV-MWAS, we conducted a meta-analysis weighted by sample size for the SNV–phenotype pairs available in at least two cohorts to integrate the SNV-MWAS results derived from different cohorts (Fig. 1). This included only the independent datasets—that is, excluding LLD2 and 500FG-APK. This analysis identified 49,346 significant and robust associations that passed the study-wide significance cut-off (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11; Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) and were supported by at least 2 cohorts based on a permutation-based robustness test (cohort permutation P < 0.05 with 999 permutations), with the same association direction. These associations involved 39,663 SNVs of 101 species and 69 phenotypes.

As a resource for further validation and hypothesis generation, we have constructed a catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/) that includes all 49,346 robust associations as well as the suggestive signals that passed the species-wide significance level (species-specific, defined by Bonferroni correction based on the number of tested SNVs within each species; Methods) in the meta-analysis and the largest cohort DMP (see examples in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5).

Most SNV associations (85.76%) were supported by two cohorts, and 14.24% were supported by three or more cohorts (Fig. 3a). Although all associated SNVs showed a similar ratio of start or stop codon or missense SNVs (17.49%) compared with the background (all common SNVs), six phenotypes were significantly enriched for start or stop codon or missense SNVs (χ2 test P < 0.05): Lifelines protein diet score, on-a-diet behaviour during the past month, thrombocyte count, waist circumference, β-blocker intake and sex (Extended Data Fig. 4). SNVs in the non-coding region may affect gene expression through upstream regulators. For example, variants located approximately 10 bp upstream of the start codon may affect the ribosome-binding site or other elements involved in translation initiation, thereby altering bacterial protein expression22. We further examined the distribution patterns of common and phenotype-associated SNVs in gene upstream regions. The common SNV count showed a drop in −10 bp regions (Fig. 3b), and the ratio of SNVs with at least one association showed an uneven distribution, with a drop at −11 bp and two peaks at −55 bp and −83 bp (Fig. 3c).

a, Proportion of gut microbial associations in different categories, including association supporting cohort number, species-level association, SNV effect and protein function annotation status. b, Count of SNVs in the −100 bp to −1 bp region upstream of the gene. The dashed line indicates the drop in SNV count at −10 bp. c, Proportion of SNVs associated with at least one host phenotype in the −100 bp to −1 bp region upstream of the gene. Dashed lines indicate the peaks at −83 bp and −55 bp and the drop at −11 bp. d, Number of independent meta-analysis association signals with gut microbial SNVs for each phenotype. Association P values were obtained from two-sided LMM tests in each cohort followed by sample size-weighted meta-analysis. Study-wide significance was defined using a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11, based on 922,497,753 phenotype–SNV tests. Exact P values for individual association signals are provided in Supplementary Table 10. Colours indicate if the abundance of the species corresponding to the signal is associated with the corresponding phenotype. e, Total number and proportion of association signals in which the abundance of the species corresponding to the signal is associated (blue) or not associated (red) with the corresponding phenotype. f, Two-dimensional density plot showing the inverse correlation between MAF and scaled effect size for the 940 independent meta-analysis association signals. g, Heat map showing the proportion of shared association signals between phenotypes. Only phenotypes that share at least ten signals with another phenotype are shown. The bottom triangle shows the proportion of shared signals between phenotypes, as indicated by colour intensity. The upper triangle shows the number of shared signals between phenotypes. AAT, α-1-antitrypsin; BA, bile acid; CA, cholic acid; CDCA, chenodeoxycholic acid; DBP, diastolic blood pressure; GCA, glycocholic acid; GCDCA, glycochenodeoxycholic acid; GDCA, glycodeoxycholic acid; GUDCA, glycoursodeoxycholic acid; HCT, haematocrit; HDL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; LCMS, liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry; LDL, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; p, proportion in total BAs; PPI, proton pump inhibitor; SBP, systolic blood pressure; TCA, taurocholic acid; TCDCA, taurochenodeoxycholic acid; TDCA, taurodeoxycholic acid; TG, triglycerides; TUDCA, tauroursodeoxycholic acid; UDCA, ursodeoxycholic acid; WHR, waist-to-hip ratio.

As SNVs can be correlated due to linkage disequilibrium in the genomes, we conducted a grouping analysis to select the most significant SNVs within each linkage disequilibrium block as representative tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 < 0.01; Methods). We then identified 940 independent SNV-MWAS signals (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 10) and 13,198 SNVs with a high probability of contribution to phenotypic variation (posterior inclusion probability > 0.8) (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Power assessment found that 70.5% of signals have more than 0.80 power to be detected given the observed effect size, sample size, and MAF (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7) and showed a negative correlation between MAF and effect size (Fig. 3f, R = −0.29, P = 6.06 × 10−20). We also assessed replication across cohorts of different ancestries. Among the 940 signals, 215 had both SNVs and phenotypes available in the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts, with 161 (74.9%) signals involving 8 different phenotypes supported by both cohorts. For example, 48 association signals of 23 species with age are supported by Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Notably, among the 940 SNV–phenotype association signals, 65.74% showed no significant associations at the abundance level (linear regression, Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis P > 0.05; Fig. 3d,e). To illustrate the added value of SNV associations, we systematically assessed the phenotypic associations with the gut microbiome at the species abundance, SNV and structural variant levels. Among the 62,464 species–phenotype pairs (Methods), 533 showed associations at SNV level, 460 (86.30%) showed associations only at SNV level, and just 5 (0.9%) showed associations at all 3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Tables 11–13). These results suggest that SNV-based analyses provide complementary information to structural variant- and abundance-based analyses when investigating host–microbiome associations4,5,23.

Among 940 signals, 810 were linked with intrinsic factors and 130 with exposure factors (Supplementary Note 7). We found 152 pairwise signal combinations involving 26 intrinsic phenotypes (excluding age, sex and height), in which the same tag SNVs were associated with 1 or more exposure factors (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 14). To assess whether exposure factors confounded the association signals of the intrinsic factors, we included the exposure factors as covariates in a robust association test using LMM-based permutation tests (999 permutations) for the association signals shared between intrinsic phenotypes and exposure factors. Owing to data completeness requirements (phenotype, exposure and SNV all had to be observed in at least 100 samples), we could evaluate 66 signals. Of these, 54 (81.8%) remained significant in at least 2 cohorts after controlling for the exposure factors (permutation P < 0.05), suggesting that the exposure factors did not confound the majority of the SNV associations with intrinsic phenotypes.

Age showed the highest number of association signals (99 signals) involving 8,117 SNVs across 42 species (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11) (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 10). We next assessed how well microbial SNVs could predict host age (Methods). To this end, we trained a machine learning model in the DMP cohort and evaluated its predictive performance in the other cohorts. The model explained 12.8–42.0% of the variation in age (R2) in the test datasets (Supplementary Notes 8 and 9, Supplementary Figs. 8–10 and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16), suggesting the predictive potential of gut microbial genetics for host age.

The most robust signal was supported by four independent cohorts (meta P < 5.42 × 10−11; Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 10). This signal contains five SNVs in the genome of F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274), and their associations were not confounded by other microbial features, including bacterial lineage, species abundance and structural variants (Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Note 10). Notably, all five age-associated SNVs are missense variants located in the sarA_2 gene (gene ID: 102274_01471). The most significant SNV was 102274_1617247 (effect allele: T, effect allele frequency = 17.38%, β = 4.93, meta-analysis P = 1.00 × 10−17), showing that individuals carrying the T allele were 4.9 ± 0.6 years older (mean ± s.d.) than those without the T allele (Supplementary Table 10). The linkage disequilibrium analysis showed that the lead SNV 102274_1617247 is linked with the other four missense SNVs (R2 > 0.2; Fig. 4a,b) in sarA_2, and significant signals were detected in all cohorts except 300OB (Fig. 4c,d). Notably, all 300OB participants are older than 50 years and show a higher frequency of age-associated alleles compared with the other four Dutch cohorts, which have younger average ages (Extended Data Fig. 9). In other words, the age-associated allele in the sarA_2 gene of F. prausnitzii_I was enriched in an older population. Moreover, replication of the association across the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Fig. 4d) suggests convergent genetic changes during host ageing in different ethnic groups.

The horizontal dashed line indicates the cut-off for study-wide significance (LMM, unadjusted meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11). P values were obtained from two-sided LMM tests in each cohort followed by sample size-weighted meta-analysis. b, Expanded view of the signal showing the linkage disequilibrium between SNVs associated with age in the OPP operon of F. prausnitzii_I. Association P values were calculated as described in a; no additional multiple-testing correction was applied to the displayed P values. c, Violin plots of the age distribution in samples with and without the age-associated allele of SNV 102274_1617247 (Alt) in different cohorts. Inner box plots show summary statistics. The centre line represents the median, box hinges represent the lower and upper quartiles of the distribution, whiskers extend no further than 1.5× interquartile range from the hinges, and data beyond the end of the whiskers are outliers plotted as individual points. Unadjusted P values were calculated using two-sided unpaired t-tests; no adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied. d, Heat map of the significance of the associations between the five missense SNVs and age in independent cohorts. P values were obtained from two-sided LMM tests within each cohort and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. #P < 5.42 × 10−11; ***P < 0.001; *P < 0.05. e, Predicted protein complex structure of the oligopeptide transporter formed by OppA, OppB, OppC, OppD and OppF. The figure shows the OPP complex embedded in the cell membrane and the tunnel-like cavity space inside the OPP complex. f, Expanded view of the OppA subunit showing glutathione (orange) and amino acid residues (red) affected by the age-associated missense SNVs. g, In silico molecular docking shows the interaction between glutathione (orange) and amino acid residues (red for Y343 and blue for others) of SarA_2. NA, not applicable.

The sarA_2 gene is a homologue of the oppA gene, which encodes an oligopeptide-binding lipoprotein with a Tat pathway signal sequence in its N terminus. The protein product of sarA_2 also forms an outer-membrane unit of an ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transporter system responsible for the uptake of oligopeptides—the oligopeptide permease (OPP) complex (Fig. 4b). We thus hypothesized that the age-associated missense SNVs may influence the function of the SarA_2 protein (also known as OppA). To test this, we assembled the OPP complex based on the AlphaFold3 prediction, including the five subunits encoded by sarA, oppB_4, oppC_4, oppD_4 and oppF_4 (Fig. 4e). This structural comparative analysis revealed that the predicted OPP structure is similar to the substrate-binding protein-dependent ABC transporter systems of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8JA7)24 and E. coli (PDB: 6CVL)25, supporting the plausibility of the predicted ABC transporter architecture. The sectional view of the predicted OPP complex structure revealed a tunnel-like cavity, with the OppA subunit acting as a gate for the transportation tunnel (Fig. 4e). Notably, the age-associated SNVs we identify are located in the cavity of OppA that relates to the tunnel (Fig. 4f), which suggests that these SNVs may affect the transportation function of the protein complex.

To infer the potential ligand of the OPP complex and better understand the underlying age-related changes in transport function, we examined the functional annotations of each subunit of the complex in detail. The OppF_4 subunit, encoded by the gene 102274_01467, was annotated as a GsiA subunit of the transporter for glutathione, an antioxidant that can prevent the damage caused by oxidative stress for both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. We then compared the protein sequences of OppA, OppB_4, OppC_4, OppD_4 and OppF_4 with 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system and found that all 5 subunits match existing protein sequences (E-value < 1 × 10−10; Methods), indicating that the OPP complex may function as a glutathione transport system. In silico molecular docking analysis further revealed that glutathione can bind to the pocket region of the OppA protein (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10). This suggests that age-associated mutations may affect glutathione uptake efficiency and help F. prausnitzii_I better resist ageing-related oxidative stress in the intestinal environment.

Motivated by the structural characterization of age-associated SNVs in sarA_2, we further systematically depicted the effect of associated SNVs in relation to protein structures. To this end, we focused on 6,799 associated missense SNVs, which are related to 3,724 proteins. We retrieved high-confidence three-dimensional structures of 2,141 (57.49%) proteins with 3,705 associated missense SNVs from the ESM Metagenomic Atlas26 and AlphaFoldDB27. We then systematically characterized these SNVs in relation to structural properties, including relative solvent accessibility (RSA, how exposed a residue is to a solvent), distance to ligand (DTL, distance from the residue to the nearest predicted pocket centre) and distance to protein–protein interaction interface (DTPPI, distance to the closest residue within a predicted protein–protein interface region) (Methods). We designated SNVs in low-DTPPI regions (DTPPI < 10 Å) or low-DTL regions (DTL < 15 Å) as structurally important28,29,30,31,32. Out of 3,705 SNVs, 752 (20.3%) were structurally important by these criteria, including 246 and 528 SNVs affecting amino acid residues in low-DTL and low-DTPPI regions, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 17). These SNVs were associated with 40 different phenotypes (Fig. 5b,c).
