The x axis shows the minimum DTL of the age-associated SNVs within each gene and the y axis shows the corresponding association significance with age. Dot size indicates the number of age-associated SNVs with low DTL (<15 Å) for each gene. P values were obtained from two-sided LMM tests in each cohort followed by sample size-weighted meta-analysis. Study-wide significance was assessed using the Bonferroni-corrected threshold meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11. e, Genes containing age-associated missense SNVs. The x axis shows the minimum DTPPI of the age-associated SNVs within each gene and the y axis shows the corresponding association significance with age. Dot size indicates the number of age-associated SNVs with low DTPPI (<10 Å) of each gene. Association P values were calculated as described in d. f,g, Predicted structure of the marR homodimer in cartoon and surface representation with the five residues with zero DTPPI affected by age-associated missense SNVs shown in red. h, Dimeric region (red) of the marR homodimer in cartoon and surface representation. i, Result of in silico alanine scanning mutagenesis analysis on two chains (A and B) of the marR homodimer. Yellow regions indicate the location of residues with zero DTPPI that are affected by age-associated missense SNVs. Residues in h and dots in i are coloured according to change in binding free energy (ΔΔG).

Age was associated with 165 structurally important SNVs in 122 genes (Fig. 5d,e). Among these, 54 were identified to be low-DTL SNVs, including 3 of the 5 missense SNVs in the OPP subunit encoded by sarA_2. In addition, seven low-DTL SNVs were found to be located near a pocket region of the serpin domain-containing protein (gene ID: 104463_01487) in Vescimonas sp900548615 (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Table 18). Previous evidence suggested that microbial serpins can inhibit host serine proteases, thereby affecting many physiological processes, such as inflammatory responses33,34. Moreover, 114 age-associated SNVs were identified as low-DTPPI SNVs, including 7 SNVs in the Vescimonas sp003539495 gene (gene ID: 102612_00172) encoding an HTH marR-type domain-containing protein located in the protein–protein interaction region (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 18). The bacterial marR homologues are transcriptional regulators that can regulate the expression of many genes related to oxidative stress response35. The marR protein functions as a homodimer, and the age-associated mutations with zero DTPPI we identified were located in the dimerization interface where the two marR monomers directly interact (Fig. 5f,g). To assess how these SNVs may influence marR dimerization, we performed an in silico alanine scanning mutagenesis analysis, systematically replacing each amino acid residue with alanine and quantifying the changes in binding free energy. The age-associated SNVs were clustered in regions showing substantial shifts in binding affinity in the alanine scan (Fig. 5h,i), indicating that they may alter marR dimerization and consequently its regulatory activity. Collectively, this structure-informed analysis highlights how integrating protein-level information can pinpoint potential functional consequences of SNVs, thereby facilitating prioritization of variants for experimental validation.

Over the past decade, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) and metagenomics-based microbiome studies have enhanced our understanding of the roles of host genetics and the symbiotic microbiome in host health. However, the application of GWASs to metagenomic data remains limited. In this study, we took advantage of the growing number of large-scale, deeply phenotyped cohorts with gut microbial metagenomic sequencing data to conduct a PheWAS on 244 phenotype and exposure factors through a gut microbial SNV-MWAS. This identified 940 independent meta-analysis association signals between SNVs of 101 gut microbial species and 69 human phenotypes and exposures. All associations are detailed in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/).

To carry out this study, we had to resolve a few technical challenges. First, metagenomic sequencing can result in a high genotype missing rate for low-abundance species when sequencing coverage is insufficient. Second, construction of a population genetic structure based on metagenomic data, rather than on isolate assemblies, is problematic owing to the possibility of within-species strain mixture within the host individual20,36,37. We thus adapted several solutions to make our work feasible and plausible. We first filtered out species with insufficient genotype information. We then retained sample pairs with sufficient overlap in SNVs to permit construction of population genetic structure based on kinship. Further, to assess whether a sample was very likely to be dominated by a single main strain within the corresponding species, we adapted the idea of phaseability37,38 to estimate the phased haplotypes on the basis of the distribution of allele frequencies (quasi-phaseability). We then retained only quasi-phaseable samples that were dominated by a single main strain for the association analysis.

Out of 940 study-wide significant signals, 482 (51.3%) carry at least one missense change. It is notable, but perhaps not surprising, that a large proportion of associated bacterial SNVs are located in the coding region but do not alter the protein sequence. It is already known from human GWASs that most single-nucleotide polymorphisms associated with complex traits and diseases lie in non-coding regions or mark synonymous substitutions39,40,41. These single-nucleotide polymorphisms have been found to be more likely to have regulatory roles in gene expression or to serve as proxies for causal variants. Although functional exploration of synonymous substitutions in bacterial genomes remains challenging, previous evidence suggests that synonymous changes can themselves affect gene expression or protein folding. Synonymous substitutions have been shown to alter mRNA structures and protein levels42, to perturb co-translational protein folding in E. coli43, and to influence translational efficiency by altering the secondary structure of mRNA in Salmonella enterica44. Future studies may explore the effect of synonymous SNVs on expression or folding using metatranscriptome or ribosome profiling readouts, along with targeted perturbations in representative isolates.

This study provides a catalogue of microbial SNVs associated with various human phenotypes, offering a valuable resource for validation and hypothesis generation. However, our resource primarily includes samples from the Netherlands, with the DMP cohort supplying nearly three-quarters of samples. This imbalance amplifies the discovery power of the DMP and raises the spectre of winner’s curse inflation in the effect sizes inferred from that cohort alone45. Although we included the Tanzanian cohort to test for replication of associations in a genetically and geographically distant population, its smaller sample size limits the power of the replication analysis. In future, more large-scale cohorts with diverse genetic and lifestyle backgrounds should be integrated to enhance gut microbial SNV-MWAS in a multi-ancestry context, especially including non-European populations46. Moreover, the biological interpretation of these signals currently remains limited. Although we applied structural biology to assess the functional importance of SNVs, we need to take several further key steps to move from association signals to hypotheses. These include identification of causal variants; molecular readouts through metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics; and phenotypic readouts of microorganisms (such as growth rate, biofilm formation and energy utilization). Looking further ahead, experimental validation will be required to confirm the underlying mechanisms, including approaches such as culturing bacterial isolates with different genetic variants on human induced pluripotent stem cell-based organ-on-a-chip models to assess the effect of bacterial SNVs on human cells1,47.

The DMP consists of 8,719 individuals and is part of the Lifelines study, a multi-disciplinary prospective population-based cohort study that utilizes a unique 3-generation design to examine health and health-related behaviours in 167,729 people living in the northern Netherlands. Lifelines utilizes a broad range of investigative procedures to assess the biomedical, socio-demographic, behavioural, physical and psychological factors that contribute to health and disease, with a special focus on multi-morbidity and complex genetics48. Microbiome data generation for the DMP is described in Gacesa et al.12. In brief, fresh-frozen faecal samples were collected from participants of the Lifelines cohort. Microbial DNA was isolated using the QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (FSK, Qiagen) by the QIAcube automated sample preparation system (Qiagen). Metagenomic sequencing was performed at Novogene, China using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 sequencer.

LLD is a sub-cohort of Lifelines that was established to explore the risk factors of complex diseases. In LLD, 1,539 individuals were included, with multi-layers of omics data collected at baseline in 2013 (ref. 13). In the current study, high-quality metagenomic sequencing data were available for 1,135 individuals (474 male and 661 female participants). The average age of LLD participants was 45.04 years (18–81 years, s.d. = 13.60 years). The average BMI was 25.26 kg m−2 (16.67–48.56 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.18 kg m−2). Microbiome data generation for the LLD is described in Zhernakova et al.49. In brief, fresh-frozen faecal samples were collected, and DNA was isolated with the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (APK, Qiagen, 80204). Sequencing was performed using the Illumina HiSeq platform at the Broad Institute, Boston. 1,135 metagenomic samples passed quality control.

Follow-up APK samples of LLD were collected for 338 individuals (150 male and 188 female participants) at a second time point. The duration between the two time points ranged from 3.33 to 3.92 years (mean = 3.53 years, s.d. = 0.12 years). At baseline, the mean age of participants was 48.2 years (18–80 years, s.d. = 11.7 years) and their mean BMI was 25.4 kg m−2 (17.6–43.3 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.08 kg m−2). At follow-up, the mean age was 51.7 years (22–84 years, s.d. = 11.7 years) and the mean BMI was 25.6 kg m−2 (16.1–37.6 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.0 kg m−2). Two aliquots of each stool sample were processed and used for DNA isolation and library preparation using two kits: FSK (Qiagen) and APK (Qiagen, 80204). WGS was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform.

The 500FG is part of the Human Functional Genomics Project (HFGP) and consists of 534 individuals. The average age of 517 500FG-FSK participants was 28.47 years (18–75 years, s.d. = 13.69 years), and the average BMI was 22.75 kg m−2 (15.09–35.43 kg m−2, s.d. = 2.85 kg m−2). The metagenomic data generation was described previously14,15. In brief, DNA was isolated from 517 and 471 faecal samples with the FSK (Qiagen) and APK (Qiagen, 80204), and libraries were sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform.

The 300OB cohort was established by Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, the Netherlands50. In total, 298 older individuals with metagenomic data (132 female and 166 male participants) with a high BMI > 27 kg m−2 were enrolled in 300OB. The average age of 300OB participants was 67.07 (54–81 years, s.d. = 5.39 years). The average BMI was 30.73 kg m−2 (26.28–45.47 kg m−2, s.d. = 3.48 kg m−2). All participants were included between 2014 and 2016. The metagenomic sequencing of faecal samples was done using a similar protocol and analysis pipeline to LLD.

The 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease cohort (1000IBD) consists of patients with IBD recruited at the specialized IBD outpatient clinic of the University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG) in the Netherlands16,51. IBD diagnosis was made based on accepted radiological, endoscopic and histopathological evaluation. The 1000IBD cohort is 60.70% female and 39.30% male. The mean age of participants was 42.61 (18–82 years, s.d. = 14.69 years) and their mean BMI was 25.44 kg m−2 (15–49.4 kg m−2, s.d. = 5.05 kg m−2).

For analysis among non-Europeans, we included 300TZFG, a population cohort of 323 individuals from both rural and urban areas in the Kilimanjaro region of northern Tanzania. This study is part of the HFGP. Metagenomic data generation was described previously18. In brief, bacterial DNA was isolated using the APK (Qiagen), and libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. The average age of 300TZFG participants with metagenomic data was 33.08 years (17.76–66.43 years, s.d. = 11.25 years). The average BMI was 24.98 kg m−2 (16.41–41.91 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.93 kg m−2).

The levels of 15 bile acids and C4 concentrations in fasting plasma were quantified by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) procedures, as previously described52,53. In brief, for sample preparation, 25 µl plasma was mixed with 250 µl internal standard solution to precipitate proteins. Samples were centrifuged at 15,800g, and the supernatant poured into a clean glass tube. The fluid was evaporated under nitrogen at 40 °C. Before measuring, samples were reconstituted in 200 µl 50% methanol in water. For the quantitative determination of bile acids, we used a Nexera X2 Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography system (Shimadzu), coupled to a SCIEX QTRAP 4500 MD triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (SCIEX) (UHPLC–MS/MS). The LC–MS/MS system is controlled by Analyst MD 1.6.2 software. Bile acids were separated with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 Column (1.7 µm, 2.1 mm × 100 mm) equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 VanGuard Pre-Column (1.7 µm, 2.1 mm × 5 mm) (Waters). Separation was achieved in 28 min using 10 mM ammonium acetate in 20% acetonitrile (mobile phase A) and 10 mM ammonium acetate in 80% acetonitrile (mobile phase B), flow 0.4 ml min−1.

The proportions of 15 bile acids (with suffix ‘_p’) were calculated by dividing by total bile acid concentration. Additionally, eight different total bile acid concentrations and ratios were calculated: (1) total bile acid (Total_BAs) = sum of all bile acid concentrations; (2) total primary bile acid (Total_primary_BAs) = sum of all primary bile acid concentrations; (3) total secondary bile acid (Total_secondary_BAs) = sum of all secondary bile acid concentrations; (4) ratio of secondary bile acids to primary bile acids (Secondary_primary_ratio) = Total_secondary_BAs/Total_primary_BAs; (5) ratio of CA to CDCA concentrations (CA_CDCA_ratio) = (CA + TCA + GCA)/(CDCA + TCDCA + GCDCA); (6) ratio of unconjugated bile acid to conjugated bile acid concentrations = (CA + CDCA + DCA + LCA)/(TCA + GCA + TCDCA + GCDCA + TDCA + GDCA + TLCA + GLCA); (7) ratio of dehydroxylated CA to deconjugated CA concentrations (CA_dehydro_deconju_ratio) = (DCA + TDCA + GDCA)/(CA + TCA + GCA); and (8) ratio of taurine-conjugated bile acid to glycine-conjugated bile acid concentrations (Taurine_glycine_ratio) = (TCA + TCDCA + TDCA + TLCA)/(GCA + GCDCA + GDCA + GLCA).

The stool level of short-chain fatty acids was measured using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, as previously described54,55.

Trimethylamine N-oxide and its precursors betaine, carnitine, deoxycarnitine, and choline were measured using LC–MS/MS, as previously described56,57. In brief, an online cleanup of the sample was carried out using an analytic column containing a C18 stationary phase, prior to its introduction into the mass spectrometer. This stationary phase did not retain the analytes, but it did retain significant matrix interferences, such as (phospho-)lipids58.

Untargeted metabolic profiling of fasting plasma samples was conducted at General Metabolics using flow-injection–time-of-flight mass spectrometry on an Agilent 6550Q-TOF system, as previously described59,60,61.

Telomere length was assessed using an automated multicolour flow–fluorescence in situ hybridization (Flow-FISH) technique as previously described62,63. In brief, white blood cells were obtained by lysing erythrocytes in whole blood with NH4Cl. These white blood cells were then combined with bovine thymocytes, which have a known telomere length and serve as an internal reference. The cells underwent denaturation in formamide at 87 °C, followed by hybridization with a fluorescein-labelled (CCCTAA)3 peptide nucleic acid probe specific to telomere sequences. They were then counterstained with the DNA dye LDS751. Flow cytometry was used to measure the fluorescence intensity in granulocytes, total lymphocytes, and lymphocyte subsets (identified by antibodies specific for CD20, CD45RA and CD57). This fluorescence intensity, compared to internal control cells and unstained controls, was used to determine the median telomere length from duplicate measurements.

Signal joint excision circles produced during T cell development (sjTREC) expression was quantified using quantitative PCR (qPCR) as previously described63. In brief, DNA was extracted from whole blood using proteinase K digestion, phenol extraction, and isopropanol precipitation. We then used TaqMan qPCR on a ViiA 7 system (Life Technologies) to quantify sjTREC expression. The qPCR was performed on 75–100 ng of DNA in a 12 μl reaction mix with 18 µM of sjTREC primers (5′-TCGTGAGAACGGTGAATGAAG-3′ and 5′-CCATGCTGACACCTCTGGTT-3′) and albumin primers (5′-TGAACAGGCGACCATGCTT-3′ and 5′-CTCTCCTTCTCAGAAAGTGTGCATAT-3′) and 5 µM probes for sjTREC (5′-(FAM) CACGGTGATGCATAGGCACCTGC-3′ (TAMRA)) and albumin (5′-(FAM) TGCTGAAACATTCACCTTCCATGCAGA -3′ (TAMRA)). The PCR protocol was 50 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 30 s. Reactions were done in duplicate. Fluorescence from probe cleavage was measured at the threshold cycle (CT). Valid results had a duplicate s.d. ≤ 1. Normalized sjTREC expression was calculated from the difference between average CT values of albumin and sjTREC.

We removed host genome-contaminated reads and low-quality reads from the raw metagenomic sequencing data using KneadData (v0.7.4), Bowtie2 (v2.3.4.3)64 and Trimmomatic (v0.39)65. In brief, the data-cleaning procedure includes two main steps: (1) filtering out human genome-contaminated reads by aligning raw reads to the human reference genome (GRCh37–hg19) and (2) removing adaptor sequences and low-quality reads using Trimmomatic with default settings (SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20 MINLEN:50).

We estimated the abundances of reference genomes in metagenomic samples using CoverM (v0.7.0)66 based on the identical reference genomes used in metagenomic SNV detection.

Structural variants were defined as within-species highly variable genomic fragments (>1 kb) across microbial genomes. Structural variants of the gut microbiome were detected from cleaned metagenomic reads using SGVFinder (v2.0)4 based on the identical reference genomes used by metagenomic SNV detection.

We characterized the SNVs for metagenomic samples using GT-Pro (v1.0.1) based on the pre-constructed sck-mer database11. In brief, a catalogue of 104 million biallelic SNVs in the core genomic region of 909 gut microbial species was initially constructed based on Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG) assemblies, the genotypes of the gut microbial SNVs were tagged by species-specific k-mers, and a k-mer-based gut microbiome metagenomic SNV panel was constructed. GT-Pro directly conducted genotyping for gut microbiota from metagenomic sequencing data by k-mer-searching and matching the genotype k-mers of the metagenomic SNV panel. GT-Pro output was further converted to SNV dosage format, with genotype indicating the frequency of the alternative allele.

We calculated allele frequencies based explicitly on the average reference or alternative allele proportions across samples:

Ri = relative abundance (proportion) of the reference allele in sample i (for example, 0.7)

Ai = relative abundance (proportion) of the alternative allele in sample i (for example, 0.3)

These values typically sum to 1 per sample if only two alleles are considered.

We then performed quality control in each cohort separately, filtering out SNVs with a high missing rate (>90%) or low MAF (<0.05) to get the cohort-specific common SNVs. We next counted the number of SNVs retained for each species in each cohort and removed species with a low common SNV number (<1,000). The manipulation and quality control of genotype datasets were conducted using PLINK2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM)67.

The genes of gut microbial reference genomes were predicted and annotated using Bakta68 (v1.10.1, database v5.1). The functional effects of the common SNVs were annotated using SnpEff (v5.1f)21.

For each species, we calculated the species-specific between-sample genetic dissimilarity Di,j measured by a Manhattan distance scaled by the number of shared SNVs within each sample pair using the parallelDist() function in R package parallelDist (v0.2.6). Sample pairs sharing <1,000 SNVs were skipped for the genetic dissimilarity calculation, and the corresponding Di,j were marked as missing values. To maximize the size of the retained sample with no missing value, we removed the sample with the highest number of missing values from the matrix in each round until there are no missing values in the matrix. We further calculated the between-sample genetic relatedness, Ri,j = 1 – Di,j, and the matrix MR containing Ri,j was used as the representative of population genetic structure. We performed principal coordinate analysis on the genetic dissimilarity matrices MD using the pcoa() function from R package ape (v5.7-1) with the parameter correction = “cailliez”.

To depict the linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure overview of each species, we randomly extracted 1,000 SNVs from the cleaned genotype dataset using plink2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM) with the parameters -thin-count 1000. We then calculated the LD as a squared correlation for all pairs of extracted SNVs using plink2 with the parameters -r2 inter-chr yes-really -ld-window-r2 0. We visualized the whole-genome LD structure using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69 with the parameters -SeleVar 2 -NoShowLDist 100000000 -OutPdf -OutPng.

The co-existence of multiple strains of a species within the host may bias the position of the sample in the population genetic structure and decrease the power of association analysis. For a given species, samples in which > 80% of the SNVs have the same allele in > 90% of the reads were considered quasi-phaseable, meaning the sample is very likely to be dominated by one strain of the corresponding species. The criterion and concept of quasi-phaseability were described before38,70.

We first manually integrated and curated the phenotypes from different cohorts and datasets to ensure the consistency of units. Each phenotype was analysed with a LMM that contained: (1) fixed effects for corresponding species abundance, age, sex and sequencing depth, and (2) a random-effect term capturing within-species population structure, with the variance–covariance of this random effect specified by the sample-by-sample kinship matrix (MR). When sex or age was the trait analysed, that variable was omitted from the covariate list. The LMM-based analysis was conducted using EMMAX (version beta-07Mar2010)71 with the parameters emmax -d 10 -t genotype.file -p phenotype.file -c covariate.file -k kinship.file -o output -Z. The association analyses were performed for each cohort and each species separately, with only the quasi-phaseable samples of the corresponding species included for the association analysis. For the SNV–phenotype pairs available in two or more independent cohorts (DMP, LLD1, 500FG, 300OB, IBD and 300TZFG), a follow-up meta-analysis was performed in the independent datasets (excluding the LLD2 and 500FG-APK datasets) using the Metal software (v2020-05-05)72 with default options (weighting cohort-based P values according to sample size). To ensure robustness and further reduce the chances of false discovery of identified associations, we conducted a permutational LMM with 999 times permutation following the Monte Carlo procedure within each cohort to assess the robustness of significant associations. Regional association plots showing LD structures on the gene regions covering the association signals were generated using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69.

The threshold of study-wide significance was determined by the total number of tested phenotype–SNV pairs (922,497,753) using the Bonferroni method: 0.05/no. of phenotype–SNV pairs = 5.42 × 10−11. Similarly, suggestive significance was determined using Bonferroni correction based on the total number of tested SNVs in each species and for each phenotype. Thus the suggestive significance did not control for the number of species and phenotypes involved in the study.

The SNVs could be correlated due to LD in the genomes. To count the number of independent association signals, we further conducted a grouping analysis that grouped interrelated SNVs by LD and picked the most significant SNVs within each LD block as representatives or tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 > 0.01, window size = 10,000 kbp) using PLINK2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM)67. The primary and secondary significance cut-offs used in PLINK2 were study-wide significance (5.42 × 10−11) and species-wide significance (species-specific) cut-offs. We visualized the local LD structure using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69 with the parameters -SeleVar 2 -NoShowLDist 100000000 -OutPdf -OutPng.

We performed a post-hoc approximate power analysis for the tag SNVs of significant associations using the genpwr package (v1.0.4) in R. The proportion of phenotypic variance explained (R2) was estimated from the observed effect size, standard error, observed sample size and MAF using the pheno_var_explained() function. Power was then calculated with power.calc.linear() under an additive genetic model and a study-wide significance threshold of α = 5.42 × 10−11. To evaluate the effect of sample size, power was also computed across fixed sample sizes (n = 100, 500, 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000) for the tag SNVs of significant associations.

As AlphaFold3 supports structure prediction for protein complexes, the three-dimensional (3D) structures of the OPP complex were modelled using AlphaFold3 (ref. 73) and visualized in ChimeraX (v1.10.1)74 and PyMOL (v2.5.7). However, according to the terms of use of the AlphaFold3 server, its output cannot be used in docking or screening tools (https://alphafoldserver.com/about). We therefore used local AlphaFold2 for monomer protein structure prediction and conducted in silico docking and other downstream analyses. To explore interactions between OppA/SarA_2 and glutathione, the protein structure of OppA/SarA_2 was first predicted using AlphaFold2 (v2.3.1)75 for both the wild-type and mutated protein sequences under monomer settings. The default reference databases and a template cut-off date of 14 May 2020 were used to guide the structure generation. For each experiment, five models were produced and further refined using graphics processing unit-based AMBER relaxation. The best model, based on pLDDT confidence scores (mean ≥ 90), was selected for downstream analysis, excluding the low-confidence N-terminal residues. The glutathione structure was downloaded from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and converted into PDB format. Ligand-binding pockets in the OppA/SarA_2 structure were predicted using P2Rank (v2.5)76, focusing on residues with high ligand-binding probabilities (>0.6) from top-scoring pockets (probability > 0.85). These residues were then used as active sites in HADDOCK (v2.4)77,78, a docking platform that generated 200 structural complexes for each variant. The top four docked poses from the best-scoring cluster were selected and energy-minimized in water. Binding free energies (ΔG) were estimated using PRODIGY-LIG (v1.1.4)79,80, and PLIP (v2025)81 was used to identify non-covalent interactions. As a docking benchmark, a literature-derived82,83 tripeptide panel representing basic (KAK, KWK, KKK), neutral (AAA, GFG, GAG) and acidic (EEE, DED) chemistries was docked to the same OppA binding site using the same set of active residues defined for the glutathione docking in HPEPDOCK (v2.0)84. All the resulting complexes were refined through water minimization in HADDOCK (v2.4)77, and binding free energies were estimated with PRODIGY-LIG (v1.1.4)79.

The protein structural property analysis was conducted using an internal pipeline (https://github.com/GArcho44/snvs-annotation-pipeline). In brief, to interpret effect of SNVs at the protein structure level, only missense variants in coding regions were retained. Functional gene annotations from Bakta (v1.10.1)68 and UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org/)85,86 enabled linkage of genes to protein sequences within UniRef100 and consequently to structure entries in the AlphaFold Database (AlphaFoldDB, v2022)27. Recognizing that many genes lacked direct matches in UniRef100, we applied a homology-based approach to expand structural coverage. Gene coding sequences were extracted using GffRead (v0.12.7)87 and translated to proteins with EMBOSS transeq (v6.6.0)88. The resulting sequences were queried against AlphaFoldDB and ESM Metagenomic Atlas (version 1 November 2022, https://esmatlas.com/)26 using DIAMOND BLASTP (v2.0.15)89, retaining only full-length matches with ≥98% identity. When multiple matches occurred, the best match was selected by identity score, preferring AlphaFoldDB entries when there was a tie. Protein accessions (UniProtKB or MGnify) were then used to retrieve high-confidence structural models (mean pLDDT ≥80) via custom application programming interfaces. Multiple per-residue properties were measured on these curated protein models to functionally annotate the structural properties of SNVs. Relative solvent accessibility (RSA) was calculated using DSSP (v3.0.0)90,91, normalizing surface exposure per residue against empirical maxima. Ligand-binding pockets were detected using fpocket (v4.2.1)92 and rescored with fpocketPRANK to boost detection sensitivity. Binding residues were defined from pockets with druggability score > 0.5. Each residue’s distance to ligand (DTL) was computed based on the minimal Euclidean distance to the closest pocket centre. Protein–protein interaction interfaces were predicted using PeSTo (model version i_v4_1)93. Residues with interface confidence scores > 0.5 were grouped into clusters based on spatial proximity (Cα–Cα < 10 Å), and only high-confidence clusters (average score > 0.8, pLDDT > 0.7 and ≥6 residues) were retained. Each residue’s distance to protein-protein interface (DTPPI) was calculated based on Euclidean distance to closest residue of predicted interface.

The 3D structure of the marR homologue dimer was modelled using AlphaFold3 (ref. 73) and visualized with ChimeraX (v1.10.1)74. Protein-protein interface analysis, specifically in silico alanine scanning, was performed using the mCSM-PPI2 web server94.

The original gene annotation was conducted using Prokka (v1.13.3)95, and the age-association signal was identified in the gene annotated as sarA (UniProtKB: P31306), which is located next to oppB, oppC, oppD and oppF. The sarA gene encodes a periplasmic oligopeptide-binding protein, SarA, and contains an oppA gene family domain. According to the literature96,97, OppABCDF is a typical oligopeptide permease (OPP) or ABC transport system complex. Therefore, sarA, oppB, oppC, oppD, and oppF could form a gene cluster whose products can assemble into an oligopeptide ABC-transport system complex.

To confirm whether the gene organization of these five genes is conserved as a gene cluster across different bacterial genomes within the F. prausnitzii taxonomic clade, we conducted a gene cluster search using cblaster (v1.3.20)98 in 17,496 assemblies of F. prausnitzii from publicly available databases such as UHGG (v2.0.2)99, SPIRE100, and our in-house F. prausnitzii MAG and isolate genomes6. We found that all 5 genes co-occur in 2,185 F. prausnitzii genomes, situated close to each other (maximum distance between any 2 hits in a cluster <20 kb). The F. prausnitzii species with the complete OPP operon are Faecalibacterium butyricigenerans (223), Faecalibacterium duncaniae (3), Faecalibacterium longum (1,568), F. prausnitzii _I (372), Faecalibacterium sp900539945 (1), Faecalibacterium sp934514285 (15) and 3 unclassified genomes. Therefore, the SarA gene and the other four genes (oppB, oppC, oppD and oppF) do form a gene cluster or operon that is conserved in its gene organization within the F. prausnitzii genome. We also conducted 3D structure prediction using AlphaFold3 for the protein complex, compared it to the experimentally derived structures, and found that the predicted structure is similar to experimentally validated ABC transporter structures in M. tuberculosis (PDB: 8JA7)24 and E. coli MetNI (PDB: 6CVL)25. Therefore, the SarA with the OppA domain can function as OppA and can assemble with the other four subunits to form an OPP complex.

To further identify the potential ligand of this OPP complex, we conducted gene function annotation with Bakta (v1.11.0)68. We found that one of the five genes in the OPP gene cluster was annotated as an ABC-type glutathione transport system ATPase component (gsiA). We then compared the protein sequences of SarA (OppA), OppB, OppC, OppD and OppF to 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system using blastp (v2.16.0 + ). We found that all five proteins match existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system (E-value < 1.00 × 10−10). The OPP complex may therefore function as a glutathione transport system.

To identify the genes from reference genomes potentially related to nicotine degradation, we obtained sequences of 92 proteins involved in two nicotine-degradation pathways from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) (KEGG entries: M00810 and M00811) and searched for them in the genes of 909 reference genomes using tblastn (v2.14.1-gompi-2023a)101. In total, we identified 2,434 genes similar to known nicotine-degradation genes (E-value < 1.00 × 10−10).

We constructed a host age prediction model based on light gradient-boosting machine implemented in the R package lightgbm (v3.3.5). To ensure generalizability of the model, we used tidymodels (v1.1.0) to conduct nested cross-validation with a five-times-fivefold split for the outer loop and a fivefold split for the inner loop to assess the predictive power of gut microbial SNVs on host age. To avoid information leakage for the samples collected from individuals with close microbiome kinship, samples from the same lineage group were assigned to the same split dataset (either internal train dataset or internal test dataset) using the group_vfold_cv() function during the nested cross-validation procedure. We defined lineage groups using all SNVs used for age model training, pooled across species. Pairwise sample distances (scaled Manhattan distance) D were computed, and kinship was then defined as K = 1 – D. From D = 1 – K, we built a neighbour-joining tree and rooted it to orient the cut. Lineage groups were assigned by a single tree-height cut at h = (1 – c)/2 with kinship cut-off c = 0.9 (thus h = 0.05, equivalent to distance cut-off 0.1). Each descendant clade crossing this cut was then treated as one lineage group. In all cross-validation runs, we used a set of predetermined hyperparameters: trees = 2000, tree_depth = 15, min_n = 30, sample_size = 0.6, mtry = round(0.2 * total_feature_number), and learning_rate = 0.01. We estimated the importance of features using Shapley additive explanation, which assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. After 5 × 5 rounds of fivefold cross-validation, we calculated the median importance value of each SNV feature, sorted the SNV features from high to low median importance values, cumulatively summed the median importance values until we reached 95% of the total sum of importance values, and took the counted SNV features as the predictive features for the final model. Because lineage groups were defined using SNVs pooled across species, this approach captures overall microbiome kinship but may not fully prevent information leakage for individual species whose species-specific kinship structure differs from the overall pattern.

The partial correlation test was conducted using the pcor() function of R package ppcor (v1.1). For the partial correlations between gut microbial SNV age and other biological age indices and between gut microbial SNV age and host intrinsic phenotypes, we used partial Spearman’s correlation, adjusting for chronological age. For the partial correlations between gut microbial SNV age and untargeted blood metabolome, we used a partial Pearson correlation, adjusting for chronological age, sex and blood creatinine level.

#1379. My Everton #178: What Makes It The People's Club

It all started with my dad who used to go to both Everton and Liverpool games well before my time.

Over the years, he started a family and, thankfully, his allegiances started to move towards Everton.

Jimmy, my eldest brother, came along years later and he started following the Blues straight away, going to the games as soon as he was allowed to.

I came along in 1984 and soon became the newest Blue in the house.

From the age of around 10, Jimmy took me to my first game at Goodison and I fell in love with Everton from that day. Me and Jimmy went to every home game and a few of the local away fixtures as well.

Our dad didn’t really go to many games with us. He did start coming again around 1999 but had a heart attack after one of the games. He never went again – but followed from the couch at home.

Moving forward some years Jimmy met his future wife, Christine, who at the time was a Leeds fan... not for long, though! It took only three games watching the Blues to convert her and extend our home seats by another.

We loved the tradition of a home game day: the meet-up at my mum and dad's house and the drive listening to Radio City’s football talk.

We had season tickets for many years until Christine became ill and needed constant treatment. We all decided to give them up and buy each game separately if and when we could around her treatment.

Unfortunately, after a year, Christine lost her battle and left us. Jimmy needed to get back to Goodison as soon as possible, so again, we all started going to every game together.

Skip through to 2024 and our dad passed away. Another blue light gone out.

Me and Jimmy made sure to remember him at the new stadium with a stone and photo inside.

Jimmy was obsessed with the new stadium build, watching drone progress daily. He waited so long for a new stadium. Unfortunately, Jimmy also passed away just two months after our dad, not getting to step inside the new stadium he always dreamed of.

Again, with losing my dad and Jimmy, who I always went the game with, I decided that I would also stop going.

For the past two seasons I've supported from home, but all while still singing the Blues!

Family is what makes Everton the People's Club.

Its love is passed down through each family member. All those years ago my dad could have chosen the red side but didn’t.

Since then, at least 15 family members have supported and followed the Blues.

I still haven't been a game at our new stadium, but Jimmy and Christine's grandkids do, singing in his name.

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1378. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

It’s all over at the Vitality, with Bournemouth recording back-to-back Europa League wins thanks to a commanding 3-0 victory over Sturm Graz. Goals from Evanilson, Rayan and Rodriguez secured the three points and Bournemouth’s first ever home win in Europe. What a special night for everyone associated with the club.

It’s the striker’s first goal for his new club after joining in the summer! The goalkeeper gets a touch on the penalty, but Rodriguez still finds the net to seal the three points and add further gloss to the scoreline.

Sturm Graz fail to clear a corner and the ball breaks to Hill. The Bournemouth man is caught by Stankovic’s sliding challenge as he goes to shoot, with his strike also hitting the visiting captain’s hand. It’s unclear which offence the penalty is for, but Bournemouth won’t care. Rodriguez will take it.

Rayan tees up Kluivert for a strike from outside the box, but the Dutchman’s fizzing shot is parried away by Khudyakov as Bournemouth are denied a third goal.

Rose makes a late change for Bournemouth as Adli replaces Gannon-Doak out wide.

As it stands, Brighton are top of the Conference League table as they’re currently winning by the biggest margin on the opening matchday. Hurzeler’s team are brimming with confidence and flexing their muscles early on in the competition.

There is a brief break in play as Soler falls and hurts his elbow. The defender temporarily goes off the pitch, but he’s okay to continue.

That triple change which saw Christie, Kluivert and Rayan introduced definitely altered the flow of this game, giving Bournemouth added energy and impetus.

How important could that goal be for the hosts? Bournemouth finally have a two-goal cushion! The goalkeeper won’t want to watch the replays of this one. Khudyakov fails to claim the corner and fumbles the delivery. The ball subsequently drops to Rayan, who squeezes an effort throw a crowd of bodies and under Khudyakov into the net. You can feel the relief inside the Vitality.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1377. Unai Emery has closed gap between Aston Villa and Europe's elite - but rampant Barcelona proved there is still a way to go as Lamine Yamal dazzles, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:17 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 11:27 EDT, 4 November 2026

John McGinn heard the question. His eyes darted around Barcelona's packed media auditorium for a second or two on Monday night. What was it like to be about to play in the Nou Camp, the Aston Villa skipper had been asked, as if this were to be some sort of spin off from Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure.

McGinn was careful with his answer. He did not seek to downplay the nature of the occasion or the thrill that comes with lining up in such a majestic arena. But he was determined not to play the wide-eyed ingenu. 'What our club is trying to do now,' McGinn said, 'is make this normal, make this a yearly experience.'

So when he and his team-mates walked up the flight of steps from the dressing rooms into the vast bowl of the stadium on Tuesday evening, they were here to show that they were not arrivistes. Villa is a historic club. They won this competition in 1982, ten years before Barcelona ever did. They were not here for a treat or to get patted on the back just for turning up.

It is nearly 20 years since Liverpool became the last English club to win here and nobody gave Villa too much chance of ending that drought. They are being told constantly that the odds are stacked against them and that their much-admired manager, Unai Emery, may be tempted by the entreaties of struggling 'giants' elsewhere.

That was the reason why this game early in the league phase had attained so much importance. For Villa, it was a symbol of something they aspire to. They want to get used to belonging in this company, to walking up those steps, to emerging into the stadium in the pouring rain, and staring at players of the calibre of Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Pau Cubarsi staring back at them.

It still feels as if they stand on the cusp of something bigger but they blew their shot at proving that on Tuesday night. They needed to be at their best to have a chance of beating Hansi Flick's side, which sits atop LaLiga, and they were far too naïve in defence to get close to causing a shock. They are rising but this was a step too far at this stage of their evolution.

Lamine Yamal (centre) and Barcelona had plenty to smile about after beating Aston Villa 3-0

Yamal opened the scoring for Barcelona after just seven minutes with this left-footed finish

Raphinha (right) doubled Barca's lead after half-time with this strike at the Spotify Nou Camp

The Nou Camp, which is still in the midst of an extensive renovation and was only about two-thirds full, was ringed by towering yellow cranes, peering down at the floodlit patch of green. From their lofty vantage point, they saw Villa get off to the worst possible start.

Only seven minutes had gone when Emery's team gift-wrapped a present for the home side. Zion Suzuki played the ball out short to Joao Gomes but Gomes panicked under pressure from the Barcelona press and the close attention of Pedri. He played the ball square without looking, straight to Yamal.

Of all the players he could have found, Gomes had to find Yamal. The Spain superstar squared up Pau Torres and then curled the ball around him with a gentle caress of his left boot. Suzuki was helpless. The ball nestled in the corner of the net. Barcelona had scored 56 goals in 14 games before this match. Extending the hand of generosity to them must have felt particularly galling for Emery.

Villa almost hit back immediately. A stinging volley from Matty Cash was deflected wide and Barcelona looked jittery at the back. Nicolas Jackson played a square ball to Johan Manzambi, who should have equalised but scuffed his first-time effort wide of Joan Garcia. Barcelona were thankful for Garcia's intervention when he raced out of his goal to dispossess Jackson as he charged on to a through ball.

Yamal was rampant. His battle with Ian Maatsen was a mismatch and Maatsen was booked after 11 minutes for hacking him down. Villa were still intent on playing themselves into trouble. Suzuki repeated his mistake when he tried to play the ball out to Joao Gomes. This time, Pedri beat him to it and the loose ball fell to Gordon. Gordon hit his shot towards the corner but Suzuki redeemed himself by diving to push it away.

Barcelona had the better of the play. They looked like scoring every time they went forward. Time and again, either Raphinha or Yamal found space to run at the Villa defence, which was barely coping. Even in that context, though, it was an open game. Villa had chances, too. Manzambi forced a fine save out of Garcia. A Jackson breakaway was thwarted by a last-ditch block.

But seven minutes after the break, Barcelona doubled their lead. Fermin Lopez played a clever ball to Raphinha, who had found a yard of space in the box. Raphinha, LaLiga's leading scorer this season, drilled a left-foot shot goalwards and it deflected off the heel of Torres, wrong-footed Suzuki and rolled over the line.

Barcelona put the game out of reach midway through the half when Joao Cancelo forced his way past McGinn on the left flank and hit a sumptuous cross into the box with the outside of his right foot. Raphinha gambled on the path of the ball, darted behind his marker and tucked the ball away.

Raphinha completed the scoreline with this cute finish as Barcelona completed their victory

For Aston Villa, this will be a learning curve as they look to go far in the Champions League

Villa manager Unai Emery will have plenty to think about after another Nou Camp defeat

Substitute Leon Goretzka hit the face of a post for Villa late on but the game was already gone. There was no shame in losing to a team who are one of the favourites to win the competition this season but there was frustration in the way Villa had handed their opponents the advantage.

Emery looked bedraggled as he stood on the touchline in the rain, arms folded, shaking his head. This was his 15th defeat in 16 visits to the Nou Camp. As Villa's coach fights to edge his team closer to the elite of the game, this game will become just one more bad memory.

#1376. Everton's Remembrance Day Plans

Everton and Coventry City will come together ahead of Friday’s Premier League fixture at Hill Dickinson Stadium to remember the fallen and honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women during conflict.

The pre-match Remembrance ceremony will involve players and staff from both clubs, as well as representatives of the Royal Navy, British Army, Royal Air Force and Merchant Navy.

Those taking part in the tribute will include serving personnel from the Tri-Service Toffees Supporters’ Club and former servicemen and women supported by Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme.

Supporters are requested to arrive to their seats from 7.50pm, ahead of the ceremony, which will follow the walk-out by the teams and match officials.

As part of the Remembrance ceremony, the captains of Everton and Coventry City will lay commemorative poppy wreaths on the pitch ahead of kick-off, along with representatives from the Armed Forces, the Tri-Service Toffees and Everton in the Community.

Players from both sides will wear shirts bearing the poppy emblem, in memory of the fallen.

We will proudly welcome the following service personnel to take part in our pre-match tribute:

The following former service personnel will also participate in the tribute through Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme:

Following the laying of the wreaths, The Last Post will be performed by bugler Andrew Manning.

As a mark of respect, the traditional pre-match siren will not sound before the teams enter the pitch, though Z-Cars will play as normal.

As part of the Club’s recognition of serving personnel, Steve McCann and Danny Jackson, both members of Tri-Service Toffees, will take part in the half-time Hit the Bar competition.

The Tri-Service Toffees is an affiliated Everton supporters’ club for those serving in the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force, whether regular or reservist. Evertonians interested in joining or finding out more about the supporters’ club should email triservicetoffees@gmail.com.

Shirts worn by Everton’s Men’s and Women’s players during the Remembrance period will be auctioned to raise vital funds to support the work of the Royal British Legion. To find out more – or to bid for a shirt – click here.

What Remembrance Means to Me – A Message From The Tri-Service Toffees

Remembrance is about remembering. It really is that simple.

Remembering the sacrifices made by so many, from the First World War through every conflict since. Not just those who served in uniform, but the families, friends, colleagues and civilians whose lives were forever changed.

It is about taking a moment to acknowledge those sacrifices, both great and small, and the individuals who made them.

Having served for over 37 years, including numerous operational tours in conflict, I don’t reflect on my own sacrifices. Those will be for others to remember when I am gone.

Instead, I remember my mum, who served in the Royal Navy, and my uncles Tony and Frank (her brothers). All three have now passed away, but each played a significant part in inspiring my own military career. I also remember the friends and colleagues who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the hope of making a difference.

But perhaps the person foremost in my thoughts is my wife, Shirley.

Throughout my military career, she has made countless sacrifices of her own, often quietly and without recognition. Like so many military spouses and families, she has carried burdens that others rarely see, whilst asking for little in return.

Their sacrifices deserve our remembrance, too.

So, when you pause to remember, think not only of those who gave their lives in service to our nation, but also of those closest to you, whose sacrifices may never have been publicly acknowledged.

At the going down of the sun and in the morning, we will remember them.

Major Anthony John Sandle RLC, Second-in-Command, 156 Regiment, The Royal Logistic Corps(pictured above with Everton Ambassador Graham Stuart)

#1375. A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC–VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

Principal component analysis of the 532 barley cultivars analyzed in this study that are colored by different groupings. Gray dots at the background represent the 19,778 globally diversified Genebank accessions29. Percentages on the axes indicate variance explained by PC1 and PC2.

a, A genomic-based germplasm network (GGNet)48 generated based on 23,609,453 filtered SNPs among the 532 barley cultivars. 430 cultivars were identified involving in network with their germplasm identity-by-descent (gIBD) value, and five independent groups were identified, including group 3 which further partitioned into three subgroups, including Chinese historic cultivars enriched in group 3-1 and Qingke enriched in group 3-3. Each colored circle represents a cultivar, while its size indicates the summed gIBD values with all its related varieties. b, PCA showing the genetic distribution of the five GGNet groups within the 19,778 globally diversified Genebank accessions29. c, Ancestral haplotype groups (AHGs) on the seven chromosomes of the 430 barley varieties that were identified involving in genomic-based germplasm networks (GGNet). AHGs were inferred by IntroBlocker pipeline50 using 1 Mb non-overlapping windows. The 20 most frequent AHGs are shown in various colors.

a, The phenotypic variation of ten agronomic traits across three years and two locations. HD, heading date; MD, maturity date; PH, plant height; SL, spike length; GN, grain number on two rows per spike (two of six rows are counted in six-rowed barley); SD, spike density; TGW, thousand grain weight; GL, grain length; GW, grain width; GL/GW, ratio of grain length/grain weight. The cultivars are grouped according to breeding periods, and the 27 exotic lines are taken as outer group. The colored circles represent the mean value, while error bars represent standard deviation (mean ± SD). b, The best linear unbiased estimation (BLUE) values of seven traits across multiple trials. Box plots show the 25%−75% interval of raw value in the box, with central lines indicate the median, and whiskers extending to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5× of the interquartile range; outliers beyond this range are shown as individual circles. Different letters indicate significant differences at p ≤ 0.05, determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Fisher’s LSD test.

The labels indicate each field trial as ‘location_year’ and the best linear unbiased estimate (BLUE) across multiple trials. The known loci with key regulatory genes underneath for spike (Vrs1) and grain characters (uzu/HvBRI1, and NUD) are marked.

The reference sequence was retrieved from a pangenome accession ‘FT333’30, which is a winter-type wild barley having the intact intron 1 of VRN-H1. Nomenclature of the spring-type haplotypes V1-1 to V1-11 are following the variants reported by Hemming et al.34. Orange dots indicate deletions present in each spring-type Vrn-H1 haplotype.

a, Working pipeline for generating the two sets of NILs. b, Homogeneity at the genomic background was identified by whole-genome sequencing. c, Graphical representation of NILs lines. PHR, polymorphism hotspot regions; SGR, Shared Genomic resource Regions.

a-b, Climatic parameters in the autumn-sown trial in Xinxiang (a) and the early-spring sown trial in Beijing (b), respectively. The average day length (bold curve), daily temperature and precipitation (blue bar) were retrieved from https://rp5.ru/. In (d), each genotype contained 12 replicates planted in rows, while row harvest each served as a measurement for HD, MD, PH, SL and GN; for the latter five traits (BM, GY, HI, TGW and GW), two-row harvest each served as a measurement, representing as 6 replicates. In (e), each genotype contained 10 replicates planted in rows, while row harvest each served as a measurement. Box plots show the 25%−75% interval of raw value in the box, with central lines indicate the median, and whiskers extending to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5× of the interquartile range. Each individual value (n) represents a biologically independent replicate. Statistical significance was estimated using two-tailed t-test.

a, Phenotype at the heading stage of heterozygous and homozygous PhyC-e plants in comparing with the wild-type plants under greenhouse conditions. Scale bar, 10 cm. b, Statistics for five agronomic traits in the greenhouse. c, Phenotype of two homozygous PhyC-e edited lines in comparing with the wild-type plants at the heading and maturing stages under field conditions. d, Statistics for five agronomic traits under field conditions. In b and d, box plots show the 25%−75% interval of raw value in the box, with central lines indicate the median, and whiskers extending to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5× of the interquartile range. Each individual value (n) represents a biologically independent replicate. Different letters indicate significant differences at p ≤ 0.05, determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Fisher’s LSD test. e, Transcriptional pattern of flowering regulation genes under short-day and long-day conditions. Gray shading indicates the nighttime duration. Statistical significance was determined using a two-tailed t-test (*p ≤ 0.05; **p ≤ 0.01; ***p ≤ 0.001; ****p ≤ 0.0001; ns, not significant; ns is not shown in the figures). Data are presented as mean ± standard error (SE). f, Fold change of flowering related genes transcription in PhyC-e versus PhyC-l on different VRN-H1 alleles backgrounds.

a, Phenotypes of homozygous PhyC-e edited lines in comparing with wild-type plants at the heading and maturing stages. Scale bar, 10 cm. b, Statistical analysis of ten agronomic traits. Box plots show the 25%−75% interval of raw value in the box, with central lines indicate the median, and whiskers extending to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5× of the interquartile range. Each individual value (n) represents a biologically independent replicate. c, Transcriptional profiles of flowering regulatory genes under long-day conditions. Gray shading indicates nighttime duration. Data are presented as mean ± standard error (SE). Significance of difference was determined using a two-tailed t-test (*p ≤ 0.05; **p ≤ 0.01; ***p ≤ 0.001; ****p ≤ 0.0001; ns, not significant; ns is not shown in the figures).

The photoreceptor PhyC functions as an upstream flowering regulator in grass species, promoting the expression of the photoperiodic responser PHOTOPERIODIC 1 (PPD1) and the flowering inducer FT1 (VERNALIZATION 3)21,22,23. The ancient haplotype PhyC-l, in combination with the winter-type vrn-H1 allele that requires vernalization, delays the transition from vegetative to reproductive growth, thereby preventing flowering (2nd panel, blue). In contrast, the spring-type Vrn-H1 variant, which carries a truncation in the first intron of VRN-H1 and eliminates the need of vernalization, enable flowering without cold exposure (1st panel, yellow). This allele in conjugation with PhyC-l is commonly adapted to spring-sown regimes in high-latitude or high-altitude regions. The East Asian-specific PhyC-e variant, which carries an F380S substitution at the PhyC locus and is consistently associated with winter-type vrn-H1 allele, promotes early flowering and supports adequate biomass accumulation (3rd panel, pink). The PhyC-e + vrn-H1 module allows barley to escape terminal heat stress, safeguard final yield, and fit to double-season cropping systems by leaving sufficient time for subsequent crops. This module has been widely selected in China’s Yangtze River basin. Notably, the haplotype combination PhyC-e + Vrn-H1 was not detected in barley natural germplasm (4th panel, dashed line). In this study, this novel module was generated either by base editing or by linkage breaking in the near-isogenic lines (NILs). It resulted in extremely early flowering and maturity, significantly reduced biomass, and undetected grain yield. This module holds potential for application in regions with extremely short growing seasons, such as those at very high latitudes or altitudes and at subtropical zones.

#1374. Newcastle Confidential: REVEALED - Players 'confused' by Matthias Jaissle's instructions, why formation tweak is a possibility, Joelinton injury worry and new transfer guru's methods explained

Published: 12:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 12:01 EDT, 4 November 2026

Newcastle’s players are ‘confused’ by what Matthias Jaissle wants from them, a source close to the dressing room has told me.

I've been told the squad remains supportive of Jaissle and there is a determination to get things right for the head coach – senior players accept there is a responsibility on them – but there is also a desire for clarity over what it is they are being asked to do on the field.

Jaissle said in the wake of Monday's 1-0 home defeat by Everton that he could not understand why the team had not followed his instructions and executed the tactics they had worked on in training. He said the plan was not to play ‘long balls’.

Sources also say Jaissle spoke to his players afterwards about their press not being what he wanted and their passing being too slow in the opposition half.

However, I have been told some players are unsure as to the playing style and strategy, and that has led to those in deep positions getting the ball forward as quickly as possible, invariably with a long pass. There are also some within the dressing room wondering why the team continues to play with a No 10 when they do not have a specialist in that position.

Another source close to a senior player says the logical solution is a return to the 4-3-3 of recent seasons. There was word from inside the training ground that Jaissle was considering such a change ahead of the trip to Crystal Palace last month, so it is not off the table.

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the system, especially as Jaissle believes he and Nico Gonzalez are not suited to playing together as a two.

Newcastle's players are understood to be 'confused' by what it is head coach Matthias Jaissle wants from them

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur (left) in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the Newcastle system

Joelinton is a fresh injury concern and medical staff will know in the next 24 hours if he is set to miss Saturday’s trip to Fulham, I can reveal. The Brazilian was feeling some muscle discomfort post-match on Monday and there is hope that the issue is related to a severe case of cramp.

However, I understand that is yet to be confirmed and, given Joelinton’s history of muscle strains, including his hamstring, no chances will be taken. The 30-year-old only returned from a thigh injury three weeks ago having been sidelined since the summer.

In better news, Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Lewis Miley are set to return for the game at Craven Cottage.

I understand Fernandez-Pardo wanted to be included in the squad for the visit of Everton but was told by staff he needed more training. The Belgian had missed the previous two matches with what is being described as a ‘tricky virus’ and only returned to training over the weekend.

Fernandez-Pardo arrived on Tyneside insisting he wanted to be used as a central striker following his £51million move from Lille. However, Jaissle currently prefers William Osula in that position and Fernandez-Pardo will likely be competing for a place out wide at Craven Cottage.

Miley, meanwhile, was also pushing for involvement on Monday after recovering from a glute issue. The 20-year-old’s return is timely given the midfield struggles of late, as well as the fresh worry over Joelinton and Jacob Ramsey’s suspension following his red card against Everton.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo is available again for Newcastle after suffering with a ‘tricky virus’

One player who almost certainly won’t come in for a start is Aladji Bamba, although we are told he will NOT be going out on loan in January.

The 20-year-old has appeared for just 27 minutes since his £30m arrival from Monaco in the summer, and he has not featured at all since September 19.

But despite potential availability issues in midfield, Jaissle does not feel Bamba is ready to start Premier League matches. That has led to a suggestion among some that he could be loaned out in January, especially as he has made only 12 senior starts in his career.

However, I understand the plan is for Bamba to remain on Tyneside and there has been encouragement with his recent performances in training.

Aladji Bamba has impressed in training of late and won't leave on loan in January despite his lack of first-team minutes

It has been interesting speaking to those who know a little more about Newcastle's new head of recruitment Tomas Amaral, who was virtually unknown in the UK before his appointment last month.

The Portuguese, 35, has been described as a 'bookworm and laptop obsessive', a meticulous talent-spotter who works long into the night. Amaral, who spent four years scouting for Benfica and was most recently sporting director at Spartak Moscow, has also spoken previously of the dangers of clubs signing good players who do not fit the manager's system.

He believes recruitment should begin with a clear footballing identity, rather than collecting talented individuals and hoping they somehow fit together. He also argues that scouts should challenge managers over transfer targets, rather than simply indulge their wishes.

Interestingly, his recruitment strategy involves two lists – one identifying players good enough for the club, the other those specifically suited to the manager's demands. For him, character and adaptability are considered just as important as ability.

He was part of the Benfica scouting team who identified Enzo Fernandez when signing him from River Plate in 2022. The midfielder was sold to Chelsea for a near £100m profit the following year.

Amaral’s arrival at least gives clarity to the recruitment structure inside St James’ Park, and he would appear to have a busy 12 months ahead given what feel like obvious areas for improvement across the pitch. I understand there is scope to spend in January should the club feel it necessary.

Beneath first-team level, Newcastle have cast their scouting net a little wider this week with two promising teenagers from Gambia arriving on Tyneside.

We understand Omar Marong and Alieu Saine, both 16, will stay for a two-week trial and train with the academy. They are products of the Today Makes Tomorrow Academy and have been identified under the club’s new global talent drive.

The pair caught the eye during Gambia’s triumph at September’s West African Under-17 Championship. Central midfielder Marong captained the side, while winger Saine finished as joint-top scorer with four goals. Neither player can join permanently until turning 18 because of FIFA regulations, but Newcastle are keen to assess their potential.

Meanwhile, the club are also set to appoint a specialist scout in Africa.

Finally, Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could soon be at the centre of an international tug of war.

The 18-year-old, born in Ashington and raised in Berwick, has been called up by Brazil Under 20s for friendlies against Japan and Singapore this month. He is the only English-based player in the squad.

Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could play for England, Italy or Brazil

But Ferreira, whose father is Brazilian and mother Italian, also qualifies for England and Italy. He has previously represented England at youth level and recently obtained an Italian passport.

I have seen him play a handful of times and there is certainly plenty of talent and potential. Interestingly, he has been operating as a No 10 at times this season, having come through the ranks as a winger.

Maybe there is a No 10 inside the club after all…
